utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry to be sitting too high. I'm suspicious about what's under this seat. That's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one administrative matter before we resume with the witness. There's an application for videolink testimony from a witness whose name isn't confidential, although the application is partially confidential, and that is the witness Dusan Loncar. The reasons are set out in a document which you should have received. Is there to be any Defence response to that application? If there's uncertainty, I don't need an immediate answer, but if I can have an immediate answer, it would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: After the break we will give you the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah. He may be a more important witness to the Defence than the Prosecution for all I know. I think both sides have an interest in the witness and you know that, as is not unusual in these cases, it is a question of health that arises in relation to his attendance rather than whether he should give evidence by videolink. The reason I ask for a fairly prompt answer is because there is videolink testimony next week and it did strike us that it may be possible to link this in with the other videolink testimony and save more than one trip to the region. And if therefore the application is to be granted, we would like to grant it fairly quickly. So if you could let me know at the break or let one of the staff know, we can deal with it. Good afternoon, Mr. Pesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry we were talking over you there, but there are certain other arrangements that have to be made on a day-to-day basis and we try to deal with these as quickly as we can when they arise. Your evidence will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to speak the truth which you took at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. When we left off yesterday, I just asked you about a reporting scheme. But before we continue today, I wanted to go back for a moment and ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: First of all, could we show the witness Exhibit P24.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Colonel, we'll bring up a document for you momentarily, I hope, and I want to ask you a question concerning the mobilisation and activation of the reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I may have given the wrong number here. I apparently misspoke. I need Exhibit 1924. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you have that on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it possible that we can have the English and B/C/S side by side? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise what that is and can you explain for the Judges and the rest of us what it is.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise this request made by the 3rd Army command seeking an approval to mobilise part of the military territorial detachment from the military district of Pristina, specifically in this document from the military district of Pristina from Urosevac, Obilic, and from the formation of the Kosovska Mitrovica VOD, the 54th Detachment Vucitrn. As for Pec, the 113th Detachment from Djakovica, from the VOD of Prizren, the 70th VTOD Suva Reka and 185th VTOD Novo Brdo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. And this document is from the 3rd Army command, which on this date in March 23rd of 1999 was commanded by General Pavkovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness the next exhibit, 1925.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, you -- can you recognise this and tell us briefly what it is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the response, or rather, the approval of the General Staff of the VJ following the earlier request that was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And this one is signed by General Ojdanic, who was the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, you as the -- the head of the military district, did you then subsequent to this receive any order or directions with regard to your job?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I must have received an order from the 3rd Army command, since I was their subordinate. It must be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Even though you don't have a document in front of you, do you recall about that time, the day before or the day of the NATO bombing, receiving direction to activate certain units or the reserve component?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to recollect. I must have obeyed the order specified in item 3, which specifies the start of the mobilisation for the 25th of March. I must have seen it through. There was no other option.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is there any doubt in your mind that you did see that through and activate or engage in the call-up on or about the 25th of March?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe I was able to deviate from the order. It is an order, a binding document. As far as I recall, we must have seen it through. I don't have the document I received here; therefore, I don't know on what day, at what time, and when it was registered in my command. And I don't have the time when it was forwarded to the military sectors, that is my orders to the sectors in Pristina, Pec, Mitrovica, and Prizren. I hope we saw that through within the deadline prescribed, although I can't recall exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say you can't recall exactly, are you saying you can't recall exactly whether you performed the action within the deadline or whether you performed the action at all?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did perform the action. I just can't talk about the exact time. Maybe we were a bit late. In any case, it says the start of mobilisation is the 25th of March at 0000 hours. It must be somewhere in the archives. There must be a piece of paper by which I ordered the subordinate military sectors to see it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, in this connection, we earlier had evidence that in wartime the military district which was normally subordinated to the 3rd Army would become subordinate to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, how does this tie -- a direct order from the 3rd Army to the military district tie in with that evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that would be -- I would argue that that's an argument that some sort of extraordinary state must have been declared or in existence at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I want to move to paragraph 17 of your statement. You mention that you had a company of military police and that the military sectors also had a platoon of military police. How were those military police utilised once the NATO air-strikes began? Did you continue to have control over them or were they resubordinated to brigades or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Military police platoons with the sectors comprised some 30 men, and they were exclusively intended to secure the command of the military district -- that is, sector. And the command can have as many as 500 staff. It can have several command posts, and those men are used to secure the command and its movements. They can secure the commander himself or parts of the command or any type of movement of the aforementioned organs along any axis or in any direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that issue of movement, you in paragraph 27 mention the transports coming from Serbia and the fact that they had to go through one of three routes. You mentioned that you had to organise armed escorts, that is military police, for all the transportation. So in addition to taking care of the command, were your military police escorting convoys or transport that were coming into Kosovo from Serbia during this time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We seem to have mixed the time-periods here. First I would like to respond to Mr. Bonomy's question pertaining to resubordination; that was his previous comment. The military district in peacetime was always subordinated to the command of the 3rd Army. At a certain point after the bombing, after the 24th of March - and there must be a document in existence - the military district was subordinated to the commander of the Pristina Corps. All the documentation supporting that should be in order. As regard your last question, the escorting of convoys, at that time I was assistant commander for logistics with the Pristina Corps in 1998, which is the most characteristic one, especially after May, until the end of that year and the beginning of the air-strikes. This was the most difficult period in my career with the Pristina Corps command. I believe paragraph 27 speaks for itself. The convoys to logistically secure the convoys for the Pristina Corps came along the three axes or directions from Serbia proper. In order to provide complete security along those lines of communication, a vehicle convoy had to enter Kosovo and Metohija along one of those three routes; from the north through Mitrovica, from central Serbia across the Varda, and in the south from the area of Bujanovci, and then they would stop and wait for military escort due to the lack of safety along the communication routes. This demanded daily engagement of the military police from the units of the Pristina Corps. It was usually the 15th Brigade military police unit that was used. They were located in Pristina. Daily they were tasked with escorting convoys to the destination and back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. That was a confusion on my part. So paragraph 27 is referring to 1998 when you were still the head for logistics with the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 19 of your statement you made a correction. It originally read: "I don't know if there was a structure in place to bring together village defence with the MUP civil defence and military." You indicated that "village defence" should be changed to read "reserve police detachments." In connection with that you told us that at the provincial level you were a member of the provincial staff of civil defence. Can you explain to us what was the job of the provincial staff of civil defence, and how does civil defence relate to the army reserve in the military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 I corrected the part referring to bringing together village defence; instead, I wanted to introduce reserve police detachments with the MUP. I did not have any knowledge on the activation of such reserve police detachments; however, I came across such people when touring my detachments and I concluded that there must have been a link to the MUP and that someone must have been commanding them. Civil defence is an unarmed type of organisation. It is tasked to take care of people and property. The coordination in place was not sufficiently clear to me at the time because I lacked a lot of information. By taking part in the work of the provincial staff of civil defence, I tried to distinguish between the reserve police detachments, which were most likely subordinated to the MUP, and civil defence, which was subordinated to the military detachment of the Ministry of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you say the civil defence were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civil defence or civil protection -- well, we cannot call them civil units. We should call them civil protection or civil defence, and they are tasked with taking care of people and property in extraordinary circumstances, in case of natural disasters, et cetera. Organisationally speaking, they are within the Ministry of National Defence. On behalf of the Ministry of Defence for the province of Kosovo, Mr. Ilic appeared. I think his office was called sector or detachment of the Ministry of Defence. It didn't have much to do with the MUP or with the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I can be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The witness said page 8, row number 19: "We should call them the civil protection units" because it is obvious that the first sentence and the second sentence are not -- don't make any sense. So he says it is not -- it was not -- it was not acceptable to call them the defence -- the defence unit -- the civil defence unit, but civil protection units. It can be clarified by the -- with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you care to do that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'll try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, were there two different bodies, one that was called civil defence and one that was called civil protection? Or was there only the civil protection unit, or staff, or whatever the correct term is?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The staff of civilian protection had specific clothes, which were usually dark blue, and it bears no resemblance to any sort of military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the job of civil protection? Were -- did they help sanitize the terrain by removing dead animals and things like that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. They participated in taking care of people, forwarding food, however, this was a specific situation in which they were engaged precisely to do that. They were asked to distribute food to Albanian refugees. We used their vehicles and their people to try and distribute food and assist the Albanian population that was fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your statement in paragraph 19, however, there is a reference to civil defence and to the provincial staff of civil defence. Can you explain to me, is there another body or organ that was called civil defence, which is different from civil protection?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for the staff of civilian protection, Mr. Ilic was one of the members who was there on behalf of the Ministry of Defence, in charge of those issues. As for defence, that was up to the territorial units, the detachments I mentioned, which were subordinated to military sectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In Kosovo, then, after the -- after the NATO bombing started, can you tell me among the Serbs, who had -- who had uniforms and weapons that were involved in protecting the territory and combatting the KLA and defending against a possible NATO invasion. There would have been the VJ, the regular VJ; the VJ reserve; the MUP and their various special units, including MUP reservists; the military territorial detachments, which many of were resubordinated to the army. Were there any other armed groups that were involved in protecting the territory or combatting the KLA, et cetera? Was there a village command, a village defence, a local defence, any other group like that? Or have I covered every one?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so. You mentioned all of the armed formations. The units of the Pristina Corps, according to the wartime formation and deployment, comprised those units and each of those units had a part of the reserve forces. The MUP units, according to their formation and deployment, had their own reserve forces. The TO units had detachments which were fully manned by reservists. That's the extent of my knowledge, and I did not come across any other armed formations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Should I have a clear picture, Mr. Hannis, of what's meant by a TO unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can ask a couple questions about that. I think I know what we're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, when you mentioned the term "TO unit," are you talking about the units under the military district or the -- those that were activated by the military sectors or the military territorial detachments? Is that what you mean by "TO units"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO units are military territorial units or detachments subordinated to the military districts. These units do not exist in peacetime. In wartime, these are territorial detachments. The company battalion terminology that is used in the corps of the units is equivalent to what is referred to as detachments in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that clear now, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I have a question for you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we could show the witness Exhibit P1968, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence opposes the use of this document. It objects to it because the Prosecutor has not arrived at paragraph 34, if I'm right, 32, 33, 34. Secondly, it's a document the witness knows nothing about, because as he says in 1999 he was not in the corps command. He doesn't know whether there was a command in 1999, and we cannot question him about a document he has never seen before, which he does not know exists, since he doesn't even know whether the command existed in 1999. How then can a document be introduced that I cannot cross-examine the witness about? For this reason, we object to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That objection is repelled. There seems a clear foundation in paragraph 32 for knowledge on the part of the witness. His statement indicates that he can give information that may be explored, and in any event the Bench can be relied upon to exclude from consideration anything that turns out to be irrelevant or inappropriately introduced into the transcript. Mr. Hannis. Sorry, Mr. Fila has more to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wish to add that he corrected paragraph 32. Please take note of that, Your Honours. He corrected paragraph 32 of his statement. The document refers to the year 1999; that's why I rose to my feet. Paragraph 32 is amended with an additional statement by the witness. To the witness's knowledge, this institution did not exist in 1999 so he cannot talk about it. Your Honours are right that this is found in paragraph 32, but the witness amended this paragraph, which is why I objected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, my determination takes account of what you've just said, Mr. Fila. So the objection remains repelled. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you that document on the screen before you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to see that document when you were proofing with us earlier in the week?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this week, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was that the first time you'd seen it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I want to go to page 2 on, I believe, both the B/C/S and the English. I have just one specific question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under item number 2 at the top of the B/C/S page can you -- well, let me ask you if this is correct. The English version says: "Task of the Pristina Corps. The Pristina Corps with reinforcements and the armed non-Siptar population in KiM," Kosovo and Metohija, "shall support MUP forces in defeating and destroying the STS in the zone of responsibility," that is the shiptar terrorist forces." Can you tell us, Colonel, what that term, "the armed non-Siptar population," would be referring to? Would that be one of the groups we talked about just a little bit earlier? Or is that something else other than the army, the army reserve, the police, the police reserve, and the military territorial detachments?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the author of this text is not a proper professional if he doesn't list the proper units. I myself fail to understand what this refers to, so I couldn't reply to your question. This is the first time I've heard this term "the armed non-Siptar population."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you aware that Serb civilians were being provided with weapons by the army before the start of the NATO campaign in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have some information about this. When the so-called district territorial defence was disbanded, the staff was disbanded, some of these old weapons no longer needed by the army were distributed to some parts of the population at their own request for their own personal protection after they had gone to Belgrade in large numbers asking for protection. But this information comes from public or general knowledge and my contacts with members of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were those persons Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a part of the last sentence of the witness's reply was not interpreted. It refers to the time when he gained this knowledge. He mentioned a time but it has not entered the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, when did you learn of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most probably when I arrived in the Pristina Corps. I arrived in December 1995, so it would have been during the year 1996 and maybe 1997. From conversations with various people in the command, with colleagues, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I would next like to show you Exhibit P1415, 1415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if you're going on to something else --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- I would like to ask what the district Territorial Defence was that was disbanded and when it was disbanded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not able to be very specific. Most probably it was in 1996 or 1997. Excuse me. It was before 1994 or 1995, because I know that General Bojovic was the chief of that provincial Territorial Defence staff, and that from that duty he was transferred to the duty of commander of the Pristina Corps. So that would be the time-frame, but I'm not sure, either 1994 or 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And what was the district Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The provincial Territorial Defence staff -- I must apologise because I don't have much information about it, but that is the command and control of some territorial units on the territory of Kosovo and other parts of the country. In the former Yugoslavia, there were staffs of the Territorial Defence, from republican staff level down to provincial staff level and then municipal staff level. But I cannot recall the precise way these were organised. General Bojovic, as far as I can recall, was at the head of that staff. After it was disbanded, he was appointed commander of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In that regard, Colonel, was the old TO, the Territorial Defence, in many ways was that the predecessor to what became in -- by 1998, sometime earlier, the military districts, the military sectors, et cetera? Wasn't that the predecessor body that was responsible for reserves and mobilisation and call-ups?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that the republican, provincial, and municipal staffs were subordinated to the Ministry of Defence, and they had those territorial units. As for what the military district and military sectors were doing, these were done through secretariats of national defence attached to the municipalities. And later on this passed under the purview of the military sectors and districts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We'd like to look next at Exhibit P1415.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, do you see that on your screen now? This is an order from the Pristina Corps command dated 26th June 1998 signed by General Pavkovic relating to the issuance of weapons or the distribution of weapons and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just a very brief objection to the translation of this document. I know this has come up before, but it's not a true translation in that it contains language that is not in the original. In the first paragraph it contains the phrase following the word "Siptar," "derogatory for Albanian," and that's not in the original document, and I think CLSS has no business commenting on documents but simply has to translate them. And I think it's offensive to this Tribunal for these kinds of documents to appear as official translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you wish to comment on that, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if the Court received it, but I know earlier in this trial that that was an issue. We had received some communication from CLSS about that particular translation. It's my understanding it is actually a subject of some debate within CLSS, even among the native Albanian speakers, about whether it's derogatory or not. But I guess I have a question regarding the other things that are not appearing in the official language. For example, RJ is noted to be war units. B/O is noted to be military conscripts, et cetera. So I guess I want to inquire, first of all, if that's my learned friend's only objection in regards to "Shiptar."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I think as a general matter if it's a matter of just explaining an abbreviation, that's one thing; but when it starts turning into comment that is controversial I think that is an extremely different matter. And I thought this matter had been dealt with some time ago but I'm now receiving fresh translations from CLSS that contain that same language, and I just don't think it's appropriate for them to be doing that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we take account of that comment and we'll consider whether any steps need to be taken to investigate the issue that's raised. It doesn't impact upon the conduct of the trial and therefore we can proceed meanwhile to use the documents that have these phrases in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly think it has no impact upon the Chamber that sits here, and I'm not concerned about that; it's the public impact of something like this that creates a sense that is probably false.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's only right to observe, though, that the matter did arise earlier in the trial and was addressed by the Trial Chamber at that stage. Documents which have been translated it would be very difficult to go through and send back for further translation, bearing in mind the demands on the CLSS for translation in the various trials that are ongoing here. So this requires some thought on the part of the Chamber and we shall let you know if any action is required.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One last thing in connection with that, Your Honour. I think Mr. Surroi testified about this issue and indicated that "Shqiptar" is the Albanian word for Albanian, but he also indicated that, yes, it can often be considered derogatory in certain contexts. It depends who's speaking to whom and in what context, and I think the Trial Chamber is aware of that and we're all aware of that, and we'll proceed accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If it's as simple as that, then it would appear on the face of it to be inappropriate for it to be included in the translation because it's a matter of debate. And -- but it may not be as simple as that, Mr. Hannis. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, in this document I would like you to look first at paragraph 1, which says: "Organise and carry out technical preparations for distribution of weapons and ammunition to military conscripts assigned to RJ," which I understand means war units, "of the Pristina Corps, the Pristina Military District, and the 202nd Logistics Base." In June of 1998, you were the head of logistics for the Pristina Corps command; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The assistant commander for logistics of the Pristina Corps. The commander of the 202nd rear base was a different person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. But you were head of logistics for the Pristina Corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware of this order at the time it was issued?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this order was issued in the staff of the command of the Pristina Corps, and it didn't have much to do with the organ at whose head I was because that was a separate entity within the Pristina Corps. This, however, is addressed to have the to the units who are to carry out certain organisational and technical preparations. Up to that time, all the units had their own weapons and equipment in their own depots. This is the first time I have seen this order, and I did not do anything about it with the organs I was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As head of the logistics, what was your relationship with the 202nd Logistics Base? Wasn't that something that fell under your purview?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The 202nd base was subordinate to the command of the 3rd Army. Our needs, or rather, the needs of the Pristina Corps were supplied by making requests to the 3rd Army, and they issued orders to the commander of the 202nd base.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you have any direct relationship with the commander of the 202nd Logistics Base, since you were head of logistics for the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no subordinate/superior relationship between us. We were equal in relation to the 3rd Army command, and we could do nothing without the knowledge of the 3rd Army command through documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me take you to paragraph 3 and the second paragraph under that item number. It says: "On the basis of the lists, call up military conscripts in small groups to the army barracks or organise distribution and issue of weapons in Serbian and Montenegrin villages. Devote special attention to security measures, secrecy and camouflage discipline in carrying out this task." Do you know why there was no distribution of weapons in villages other than in Serbian and Montenegrin villages?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't wish to be misunderstood because in paragraph 1 of this order I saw that only organisational and technical preparations were being carried out, and yet your question is about what I was just saying. As far as I know from day-to-day life in the area, they were asking the army for weapons for their own personal safety, especially in areas with a majority Albanian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, are you saying that this is only an order to prepare and not actually distribute?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understand it, but I have to say this is the first time I've seen it. My organs did nothing in relation to this task. Where weapons are concerned, the chief of the technical service was subordinate to me, at the request of a unit of the Pristina Corps would deal with the supply of weapons and ammunition. We were not waiting for the year 1998 or June in order to supply the units according to the establishment. No one could have more weapons in their depot than was envisioned by the establishment and the various military specialties listed in the establishment. My services and the other organs in the other services had completed those tasks long before. It was the corps command that decided what was to be done and when. It was up to us to carry out occasional checks to see how the weapons were being stored in the depots. We were checking the technical aspect. Other organs were in charge of making -- checking how these were guarded and checking other aspects of this whole issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, I believe you did get a chance to look at this document earlier in the week during proofing, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 4 says: "Conduct the issuing of weapons and ammunition in keeping with Rules on Materiel Management." That would seem to suggest that this was more than just preparation but it was going to be actual distribution.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think this is an instruction as to how the distribution is to be carried out, I assume after some kind of signal is given; and the procedure envisioned is one that my organs, the technical service, and the financial service prescribed, the manner in which equipment and materiel is issued. There were unified forms to be filled out when a conscript reported to do his military service or reservists to serve in a military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 6 says that: "After completing the distribution, prepare and organise inhabited places for defence. And the military departments commanders are responsible for organising this in their zones of responsibility in cooperation with the MUP and local self-government organs." You did not become head of the military district until January of 1999; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The district, yes, the commander of the military district in January 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in number 6 my --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I can tell you -- may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I didn't find any of this there, that something like this had been done. There was a period of about a month or a month and a half before the aggression when I was able to visit some military sectors once and others twice in order to see for myself what the situation was, the combat-readiness of those units, their familiarity with documents, the peacetime documents regulating actions carried out in wartime. I have no information that any of this was implemented, preparing villages, fortifications, and so on. At that time, the commanders of the military sectors were only asking to be replenished with materiel they needed, newer uniforms, and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next item in number 6 says: "Form units in each village according to the military structure." Did you after you became head of the military district visit the Serbian and Montenegrin villages in Kosovo to see whether or not units had been formed of villagers who had received weapons?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't know about this document and I cannot offer any thoughts on the situation in the field. And none of it was mentioned to me by any of the military sector commanders in respect of any of this being implemented. I have to say, though, that I didn't tour their warehouses, their depots. I wasn't able to see whether their weapons were there or whether the weapons had been distributed, and I was never informed of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there doesn't appear to be any indication in this order, does there, Colonel, about under whose authority these village units were going to fall?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Number 8 says: "I forbid formation and engagement of any volunteer units, except those comprising local village inhabitants." If the local village inhabitants so armed with weapons formed a unit that -- some kind of volunteer unit, under whose authority would they be, the army's because they'd received the weapons from the army? Or the military department?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely, if they were founded indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll leave that. Let me move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, you're a military man of some experience. You've given a possible interpretation of this document that would suggest it was simply instructing preparations be made and setting out a scheme which might be followed when a signal was given. Would you look, now, please at paragraph 10 and tell me how that might fit in with the explanation you've given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, reading the first paragraph, that was my conclusion; but reading paragraph 10, now I realise there were deadlines. That is why I say I see this order for the first time. And on the distribution list you have a number of items. But I have never seen this. When reading the first paragraph, it appeared to me as some sort of preparations, but now having seen that there were deadlines it is most likely that someone was ordered to do that within the time prescribed. I have no knowledge of that, and I didn't see any of it in the field during that month or so, or rather, from the moment when I took up my duties and the moment when the aggression began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move, then, to paragraph 26 of your statement. You mentioned that in 1998 the Pristina Corps had a forward command post in Djakovica, and at that time Lazarevic as the deputy commander was posted there. You say that you were never in Djakovica and: "Pavkovic held that against me." Now, how do you know he held that against you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a comment I made, or rather, that's what the word was among my colleagues when we met for daily briefings; and I believe that Mr. Pavkovic himself knew that my place wasn't to be there. And according to the then and now rules, the assistant commander for logistics never goes to the so-called forward command post. What is found there is parts of the units of the command, whether it is the command of a brigade, division, or army. And the assistant commander for logistics forms the rear command post, which is much different from the forward command post. There were some specific instances and with the view of the proper functioning of that organ headed by General Lazarevic, whereby I always had someone from the important services there, from the basic services, and I kept rotating them. There was always either someone from the technical department or from the quarter-master's office or from the medical unit. One of them was there always at any given point. Therefore, these were rumours, although it may have applied to the other colleagues of mine who didn't understand that I had to be at the rear command post in order to secure supplies for them in order it that they could receive them in time, irrespective of their location.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to move to paragraph 31. You had mentioned that you were unhappy about the situation in Vucitrn because you found one of your detachments had been split into smaller groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we show the witness Exhibit P1988, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you also mentioned you were displeased because your artillery battalion under the 37th Brigade was engaged to provide security for the VJ. You spoke a bit about this yesterday. Can you tell us what this document is. It's dated the 23rd of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We've dealt with this yesterday, I believe, when we talk about an improper engagement of the military territorial detachments. For example, the instance here was the use of the anti-aircraft artillery battalion which was part of the 15th Brigade. In this document, the commander of the 549th Brigade explains how he used the military territorial detachments within his area of responsibility. That was his decision. However, if they had been subordinated to him, he decides on their use. As I said yesterday, when I went to Prizren, I didn't come across Mr. Delic but I managed to find his deputy and we had a discussion about this. He was the person who praised the ability of the detachment, and I was content to hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there anything improper about what's in this order? It just appears it's relocation of the territorial detachments from the populated areas. Was there anything wrong about that per se?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In essence it wasn't improper. He was responsible for the entire AOR. As to how to use the given units, it is up to the commander, and on this occasion he used them, he used the detachments they way he deemed fit. Whether the members of the detachment liked it or not, well, it was his decision. What my concern was that they were insufficiently trained to perform such tasks. However, they were successful in completing them, and I believe General Lazarevic on one occasion praised this particular -- that detachment from Djakovica which had been subordinated to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 33 you make reference to the operations officer Djakovic. What was his first name and his rank?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His rank was that of a colonel, his last name Djakovic. I cannot recall the first name. He was assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training. I believe that was the proper title.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that he wrote daily reports compiled at the information processing centre. Is that -- is that the body that would issue combat orders from the Pristina Corps during the time of a state of war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the regular practice that units forward daily operative reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. What time does that refer to? Should my -- could my learned colleague tell us what year, what day, and what body we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this particular question, Mr. Fila, is quite clear. The question is whether the information processing centre is where combat orders were issued in time of war, so we're talking about the period from March -- the middle of March 1999. Could you answer that question, please, Mr. Pesic -- Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for interrupting. You are correct; however, I understood Mr. Hannis linking this question to Djakovic himself, and it is another issue whether Djakovic was at that post at that time. Therefore, we need that clarification. You are correct as to the body referred to, but it refers to Djakovic directly. Perhaps my learned friend from the Prosecution could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary, Mr. Bakrac. You can deal with the matter in cross-examination. This particular question is a more general one, and that is whether the information processing centre was the place at which combat orders were issued. Can you answer that, please, Mr. Pesic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are talking about 1998 when Djakovic was at this position. He was assistant Chief of Staff for operations and training. The standard practice is that units forward their daily reports to the operations centre with the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me break it down. In your original statement in paragraph 33 you said the Joint Command did exist in 1999. However, in your supplemental information you informed us that that was a mistake and it should read the Joint Command did exist in 1998. That was a change you made to your statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 33 it should be 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. And we noted that in your supplemental information. In 1998, when Colonel Djakovic was operations officer at the information processing centre, was he writing reports for the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I was in the centre almost non-stop, as well as Colonel Djakovic. The duty to collect daily reports lay with the officer on duty at the operations centre. In terms of structure, the operations centre was subordinated to Djakovic. As for the drafting of the daily reports, the duty operations officer would usually do that. Often, however, Djakovic himself took part as well. He asked information from me, and I secured information pertaining to the logistical support of the units of the Pristina Corps. To whom Djakovic forwarded the summary of the reports, I don't know. In standard procedure it should have been sent to the command of the 3rd Army, to which the corps was subordinated. The extent of my knowledge and me hearing that there was a body coordinating the tasks of the police and the military, well, he must have had similar information. And that body must have had similar information. That's why I conclude that Djakovic must have been sending information to them as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you said you did not see a copy of the report. You're talking about these daily reports?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the report authored by Colonel Delic [as interpreted], well, reports were typed out at the computer centre. I wasn't present during that stage. We didn't discuss this Joint Command document, but it was always there between the lines; and back in 1998 I expected that there would be some improved, some better, coordination with the MUP in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you to clarify something. Your answer was translated as saying "in the report authored by Colonel Delic." Did you mean Colonel Djakovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My original question was, though, you say you didn't see the report compiled by him. You never saw any of those daily reports he was writing at that time in 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need. I worked on my part of the report pertaining to the logistics support of the units, be it via reports or requests made. He would then collect information from the other bodies within the command, and the drafting of the document was done in our information centre, or rather, information technology centre.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The actual expression used by the witness is the information processing centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Let me move on, Colonel. Paragraph 38 of your statement you mentioned when the war started you saw large movements of people. And the English next sentence says: "I personally tried to prevent a convoy from Obilic of 3 to 400 people." I don't know if that is a mistranslation. What did you try to prevent the convoy from doing? Does that mean you tried to prevent them from leaving?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when this was. After the NATO bombing started?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, although I cannot recall the month. Maybe late April, early May -- well, late April most likely. I came across that convoy that was moving along the axis of Obilic-Slatina and onwards towards Urosevac and Skopije. When talking to the people at the head of the convoy - and there were several vehicles there as well - they told me that they felt insecure, unsafe, and that's why they wanted to leave. I asked them not to go because safety was poor elsewhere as well. I saw women, the elderly, children, and I persuaded them to take a turn towards the first village, and we met at a junction. They listened to what I said and they went down to that village. The agreement we reached was for me to go to Obilic, to the MUP there, to investigate. The reply I received from the few people I met at the police station was that they knew of that as well and that they were unable to keep them. I learned that the convoy was headed by the former municipal president of Obilic municipality; he was a well-known figure. And it was precisely he that I talked to. He was quite assertive. He seemed to be a serious man, an intellectual even. They said they had spoken to him as well, and I told them I -- that I was able to divert them for a while. I returned after an hour or an hour and a half, but they were no longer there. They went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Zecevic is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's again the transcript. I believe the witness said in 31 -- page 31, row second -- rows 2 and 3: They said they had spoken to him as well, and they were unable to divert them as well. I mean, it can be clarified with the witness because this is not what he said. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Pesic, is that consistent with what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes -- well, even the MUP was unsuccessful in trying to persuade them to stay because the former municipal president figured as the leader, and he persuaded them to follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Is this an appropriate time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We have to break at this point, Mr. Pesic. Again the usher will show you where to wait for the next 20 minutes or so while we have our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll resume at five past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, we're just talking about the convoy from Obilic and your conversation with the MUP. In that paragraph, paragraph 38, you mentioned: "I also listened to comments from people in the military territorial detachments that the people were leaving in an organised manner." When did you hear these comments? Was this on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have already told you that in the course of a day I would visit more than one detachment, maybe two or three, depending on the direction I was travelling in, Mitrovica, Pec, Prizren, so depending on the direction. There were various comments I heard, but ones I liked especially, which is why I mentioned them here, was that many people regretted that entire villages were leaving and entire neighbourhoods in Pristina. There were individuals who were embittered because they had good friends among those people, colleagues from work. For example, in Kosovo Polje. After the departure of those people, some socially owned enterprises were no longer able to operate. So people expressed concern about those departures. They weren't really familiar with the situation, so they were asking for information. Why were these people leaving? Was it under pressure? And various comments were made by members of the detachments. And they were saying that these people were leaving in an organised way, that they had prepared this departure earlier, previously, because they were leaving successively in organised groups. There were many cases where people regretted their departure because they had been neighbours for a long time. They had friends. When I mentioned the attempt to create a Siptar detachment in Dobrevo, I saw Serbs in conversation with these people in my presence who were trying to persuade them. And some of those people left on the same day. And on the following day more left and a large number had left by then in spite of the efforts of their neighbours to convince them to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Pardon my interruption, Colonel. I think you've answered my question. I take it, then, you said you were travelling throughout Kosovo visiting your detachments. Did you hear these comments about people leaving in an organised manner throughout the entire province? Did you hear that everywhere you went?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended. In some places there were comments about people leaving. In other places they were not in a situation to leave. When my members went to visit their families, they would hear that people had left the village. They would also get information that people had left and then come back, and then again there were cases where those who had returned were alleged to pose a threat to the Serbs who had stayed. And there were requests by people to be able to go home and protect their homes. So there were various kinds of situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In the course of your travels around Kosovo to visit your detachments, did you note that there were a number of Kosovo Albanian villages that had been, if not completely, largely destroyed and that there was no one living there anymore?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to come upon deserted villages. I was in charge of communications. I was in a civilian vehicle with one or two policemen from the reserve forces who were assigned to me, and we stuck to the main roads for reasons of personal safety. That's why I did not leave the main roads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter corrects herself. The witness did not say "I was in charge of communications," but "I was using the main roads."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't see any deserted or --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just one intervention. I think that the witness said "two policemen from my units." And here we have "two policemen," so maybe that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, you said that you were in a civilian vehicle with one or two policemen, and you said which units they came from. Could you tell us that again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so, from my police. In the command of the military district, there was a reserve police unit and I travelled with one or two of them in a civilian vehicle for security reasons. The establishment vehicle which was olive-green or olive-grey, I did not use it; that was a camouflage vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have occasion to travel on the main road from Djakovica to Decani during your visits?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. I did not travel on the main road from Djakovica to Decani, especially because I had only one territorial company in Decani because the number of Serb and Montenegrin inhabitants were so small. Therefore, this company was attached to the detachment in Djakovica. So I was able to see that in Djakovica, not in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about between Djakovica and Prizren?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And doesn't the main road pass --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me. Djakovica-Prizren I wasn't there because the command post of the 544th Brigade -- 549th Brigade was near Djakovica. And there I met the deputy commander of that brigade who informed me about the detachment in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you live in Pristina during the war months?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first 15 days the command of the military district was located in the municipal building of Kosovo Polje. For security reasons, the command was relocated to the library in the centre of Pristina until the end of the war, that was the provincial library.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you staying at the command during those first 15 days in Kosovo Polje?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All 15 days in the command, in the building of the Kosovo Polje municipality. I saw many reasons to provide a more secure location for such a large command, and therefore, I issued the decision that we should relocate to the building of the provincial library in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 39 of your statement you indicate that you were staying with relatives in Pristina when you heard shooting during the night. At what time-period was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't pin-point it. For security reasons, the members of my command did not stay in the provincial library building around-the-clock; they all had quarters in Pristina and most of them were permitted to leave to avoid having a lot of people concentrated in one spot because of possible bombing and losses. A minimum number of people remained in the library building. I myself spent little time in the command, except for the morning briefings with my associates, and then people would go off to carry out their tasks. At night, I spent very few nights in that building, but in the neighbouring buildings I had friends, relatives, officers of the reserve forces, reserve officers, belonging to my command. I would spend the night with some of them, escorted by my police; from time to time I would spend the night there. And on more than one occasion I experienced what I describe in paragraph 39. We were helpless. There was nothing we could do. That would happen late at night. You would hear the sound of vehicles arriving, stopping, followed by shooting, perhaps the shattering of glass or something breaking, and then the vehicles would leave. And in the morning we would find out that this had been an ordinary robbery. And I concluded that in the course of the day, by day-time, some extremist elements would be observing a store, for example, with goods they were interested in, and then by night they would arrive, shoot into the air so that nobody would look out of the windows, and it would be then easier for them to do what they wanted to do and leave. There were Albanian residents in those buildings, people I knew. I'm referring to the buildings where I spent the night. We would run into each other in the entrance-ways, when entering the building, for example, not often in the evening, but in the morning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What part of Pristina was this in? Do you know the name of the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the very centre of Pristina. The library is right in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And if I understand your earlier testimony, this would have been some 15 days after the NATO bombing began. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No, not 15 days, but after 15 days I relocated. Perhaps 25 or 30 days after the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Where -- can you tell me where you spent the nights the first 15 days of the bombing.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first 15 days in the building of the Pristina municipality, or rather, Kosovo Polje. I apologise. In the offices of the Kosovo Polje municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In those first 15 days, were you travelling around visiting your detachments in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you then transferred or relocated to Pristina after those first 15 days, did you notice that the overwhelming majority of the Kosovo Albanian population of Pristina was no longer there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that information because I wasn't concerned with Pristina. Pristina is a large town and I did not go into the various neighbourhoods of the town. It's a large town. I didn't have any reason to walk around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you hear from your relatives or anyone else in Pristina about what had happened to the Kosovo Albanians who lived there at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building where I went to see relatives and friends, there were Albanians. I heard that in conversations with my men who said that groups from certain parts of town would suddenly turn up as if under orders at the entrances to their buildings with their luggage all ready. They would suddenly turn up on the street as if in response to a signal and set off, most often in the direction of the Kosovo Polje railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you also hear that they were assisted in setting off to the railway station by the police?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From those conversations, I heard that for their own security it was observed that there were policemen around here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me leave that topic, Colonel, and before I continue to the end of the statement I have to go back one time to paragraph 32. This is where you say: "I know the Joint Command was set up in 1998 to coordinate the VJ and the MUP." You mention attending a meeting at which Mr. Milutinovic was present, along with General Lukic from the MUP and other individuals from the VJ and the MUP. In your supplemental information you tell us that you were invited by General Pavkovic to this meeting. Do you recall approximately when that meeting was?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall the time. I can be mistaken by a month because it was quite sudden. I was summoned and I think that there weren't any associates around at the time. He called me to come. I think he didn't want to be on his own; that was the impression I had. And it is very hard for me to pin-point the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember how many people approximately attended this meeting? Are we talking about ten or a hundred?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than about 20. I didn't recognise anyone there. General Pavkovic sat in the front row; he greeted the people he knew. I found a seat in the third or fourth row. It was a small hall. There weren't more than 20 people in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say in your statement that General Lukic briefed Mr. Milutinovic and then Mr. Milutinovic addressed the audience, but you don't recall what he said at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Mr. Lukic briefed Mr. Milutinovic and welcomed him, I concluded that he was their guest, because in the nature of things General Pavkovic was senior in rank and it was not usual for a junior to welcome someone. So I concluded that Mr. Milutinovic was a guest of the MUP, and that's why he was welcomed by Mr. Lukic. Of course we all rose to our feet. They shook hands, and Mr. Lukic sat down next to Mr. Milutinovic at the high table.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Milutinovic was the president of the Republic of Serbia at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you ever met him before?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Wasn't this rather a special occasion for you, to be in the presence of the president of your republic at such close proximity?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was honoured to be invited by Mr. Pavkovic. I saw the president of the republic in the flesh.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you don't recall anything he said?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven years have elapsed since then, but the issues he dealt with all related to the political and security situation in the republic and how it was reflected on the situation in Kosovo. That's my attempt to paraphrase it, but I certainly could not recall the actual words he used.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. In paragraph 40 you make reference to the army helping people and giving them food, and you talk about civilians from Istok and how the detachment and municipal leaders had helped people return to their villages. You speak in some detail about that Istok incident earlier in your statement, but you said you believe that the MUP may have spread rumours about the detachment there and the alleged setting up of the camp. Regarding the relations between the MUP and the VJ, I would like to show you an exhibit; this is P196. Did you know the chief of police in Pristina in May of 1999, Mr. Janicevic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally. I did not know any of the leaders of the MUP personally or in an official capacity. I didn't have any need or duty for any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour. Objection to the use of this MUP -- these minutes. The witness is an officer of the Army of Yugoslavia. These are minutes of a meeting held in the MUP staff for Kosovo not attended by any officers of the Army of Yugoslavia. And the meeting took place in 1991. I fail to understand how documents can be tendered through these -- this witness that have nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the 1991 is a misprint for 1999, which also appears as a date on the document. You'll see it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1999, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But that's the MUP of Serbia. This document has nothing to do with this gentleman. He's not a policeman. There is no basis in any part of his statement or the addendum to his statement. I don't know where this is leading. I assume that the OTP can find a policeman to whom to show these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Mr. Fila. However, a sufficient foundation has been shown in principle for reference to matters or documents dealing with the MUP in view of the responsibilities the witness had for MUP reservists. And I've already indicated that should something -- should it later emerge that the witness has nothing valuable to say about the document, we are perfectly capable of excluding it from consideration. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Colonel, can you see that document on your screen. Did you have a chance to look at that earlier in this week when we were proofing, in anticipation of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our proofing, yes, during our proofing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Could we go to page 8 of the English and I believe it's page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. Colonel, this is under the heading of the chief of SUP in Pristina Colonel Bogoljub Janicevic is speaking. And Can we go to page 9 of the English and I think we're still on the right page of the B/C/S if we can scroll to the bottom of that page. Mr. Janicevic is speaking and one of the things he's talks about is "cooperation with the VJ is poor." Can you locate that on the page that's in front of you? I can't read Cyrillic well enough to find it myself. There's a mention of a Colonel Cirkovic in that particular bullet point. I don't know if you see his name on that page. We're trying to make it a little larger for you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you scroll down a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, it's the 17th line from the top in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't see it on my screen. Further down. The other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you see it, Colonel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And right below that he says: "There are many problems in connection with active-duty and reserve VJ soldiers. They drive around in vehicles without licence plates and have items whose origin is unknown." Next bullet point: "The military is not taking sufficient measures and most crimes are being perpetrated by VJ members, and volunteer units with VJ uniforms must be disbanded." You were in Pristina at the time, and were you aware of any of these problems that Mr. Janicevic is talking about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That particular area is within the AOR of Colonel Cirkovic. I have knowledge that there were some mixed composition units in that area, even part of my police took part, and I don't believe this particular sentence is the best one one could make stating that there were problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How would you state it then. From your position and your view, how was the cooperation between the VJ and MUP in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally I didn't have much contact or any need for such contact of that nature. I don't have any information from the field, from the military sectors. I think the cooperation was sufficient. In the reports I received, I have no further knowledge of that. As for the area that I moved within, within the area of responsibility of the 15th Brigade, I don't think there were any problems there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what happened the suggestion that VJ members were perhaps engaged in some kind of inappropriate activity? It sounds like the suggestion is that they are driving stolen vehicles with stuff in it that no one knows where it came from. He seems to be suggesting the VJ is involved in looting. Wouldn't you be concerned about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any such knowledge. I am quite certain that ... the standing formations of the Pristina Corps didn't do that. I know that the officers at check-points did their jobs well, and I had problems crossing a check-point because our policemen could be too assertive, too emphatic. They wouldn't realise that I was one of the commanders. They wouldn't let know who to let through or not, and there was an incident involving myself in the area of responsibility of Colonel Cirkovic. Apart from that, I don't have any other knowledge, especially pertaining to any possible use of vehicles when looting. All the vehicles had stickers or symbols on them as vehicles that had been mobilised for the use of the military. A few luxury personal vehicles may have been used to transport such goods, but as for any transportation vehicles, well, I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I see Mr. Ackerman is up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's too late with regard to this question, but I think the question was improper and argumentative when Mr. Hannis suggested that the language seemed to indicate looting. I think that may be is one thing it might indicate, but certainly not clear in that regard. I think it's argumentative and leading and -- although I can't object to that because it's already been answered, I would hope that Mr. Hannis would be more careful in the future about leading and argumentative questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think you mentioned that, Colonel, to us in proofing that there was a procedure whereby during the state of war the army could - I'm trying to think of the word - appropriate vehicles for military purposes. Is that correct? Requisition?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. I had understood you to say I think that during proofing you mentioned that there was a procedure whereby during a state of war the army was authorised to requisition or appropriate civilian vehicles or private company vehicles for purposes of the military's use.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It is a planned activity to provide sufficient number of vehicles for the units. That planned activity is implemented by military sectors in order to meet the needs in this case of the Pristina Corps and the needs of the military territorial detachments. In peacetime what is planned for are the vehicles to cover the need for mobilisation and, if needed, private citizens or companies can provide their vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Colonel --

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a planned activity in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, and that is in your statement in paragraph 14. I forgot where I had seen it before. Finally, paragraph 41 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you finished with that document, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
