utterances.text: Well, that particular document will not be admitted because the witness has indicated no knowledge of the events that are referred to in it, and there should be no doubt about its lack of any positive assistance to us. The parts that were necessary for your questions were adequately quoted in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should indicate that the number is 1996; I think it was listed as 196. But for purposes of the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've certainly got it noted as 1996. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're straight then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 41, Colonel, you mention on the second day of bombing you got information about two bodies in an industrial zone where one of your units were located. Did you write a report about this, these bodies that were discovered in the area secured by one of your units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to provide security for important facilities, a unit of mine, an engineering company, which is a non-combat unit armed only with infantry weapons, was used in the area of the -- in the industrial area of Pristina. A large number of warehouses can be found there, such as those of the UNHCR, the Red Cross, the Medecins Sans Frontieres, the Mother Teresa organisation, as well as many other companies from Serbia. I decided to provide that security by using that company of mine in order to prevent any theft or looting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but we really have to make a little more progress here. And the question was: Did you write a report about this. Can you answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. That company's commander reported to me that upon their arrival they came across two corpses. He didn't know what to do with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I must -- I must insist that you answer my question which is: Did you write a report about it, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis can now follow up if he wishes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What do you know about the bodies? Were they men or women or children?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the report of the chief of security whom I sent to investigate, these were two male corpses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you know -- did the report indicate the ethnicity of these two dead males?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of security's conclusion or assumption was that they were Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were they dressed in civilian clothing or some type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did he -- was he able to observe any kind of wounds or possible cause of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But in my contacts with the MUP I insisted that they deal with the case because it was not within our competence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if the case was ever solved or any perpetrators arrested?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The case was taken over by the MUP once my chief of security submitted his report. As to the fate of the case, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm finished. I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. We've had an indication of the time that's likely to be occupied in cross-examination. I think we should indicate now that having taken account of what the witness has actually said in the time consumed that may be of significance for the trial, it's appropriate for us to indicate an outside limit that we feel is reasonable for cross-examination. And looking at where we are today, we've got the rest of today and the first session tomorrow, and that would seem to me to fit in reasonably with the requirements of cross-examination. So, please, would you reflect that in your efforts to allocate time and priorities for cross-examination of the witness. You don't have to take as long as that, of course, I urge you to remember. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will go first, followed by General Pavkovic, General Lazarevic, General Lukic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Colonel, my name is Eugene O'Sullivan, and I represent Mr. Milutinovic. Good afternoon. Colonel, I really only have one question for you, or seeking your assistance, if possible, on one matter, and it has to do with whether or not we can establish the date of the meeting where Mr. Milutinovic was present and you were present in the MUP building in 1998. I know you've said today that you cannot recall the date and your statement says that it maybe was May or June 1998. And I realise that a lot of time has gone by, but we have heard evidence in this case which I will put to you in the hopes that it may jog your memory and you can tell me whether it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And for the record, I'm referring to the evidence of Dr. Dusan Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to suggest to you that the meeting occurred in September 1998, and I'll tell you why I'm suggesting that. At the beginning of September of 1998, in Glodjane near the Radonjic lake there was a killing of approximately 30 people by the KLA, which made big news. Do you recall that event in September -- at the beginning of September 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was probably during the time when I was at the centre of the Pristina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Right. But does the -- does the beginning of September sound like the right time to you that the people -- the bodies were found in the canal that leads to Radonjic lake? Does that sound about right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the proofing with the Prosecutor in the last few days, I stated that on occasion I could go wrong as much as two months. Sometimes I worked around-the-clock and 1998 was far more difficult for me than 1999 was and I cannot pin-point the exact time. However, I was able to establish here today and yesterday that I could go wrong as much as two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we look at it more simply. Do you remember the event Mr. O'Sullivan has referred to, the killings at the Radonjic lake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it, Mr. O'Sullivan, you could try to use that recollection to jog the memory, but it doesn't follow that the witness needs to remember the month.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Colonel, I want you to understand that we're not -- and I'm not criticising you in any way for having perhaps lost track of time, but I'm suggesting to you that the visit of Mr. Milutinovic to the area on the day that you were at that meeting was in the latter part of September. And the reason for his visit was a one-day visit to Pristina and the area where in fact he visit Radonjic lake and laid a wreath of flowers. And at one point in that day-trip he was in the MUP building in Pristina and that's the event you recounted in your evidence. Does that refresh your memory, and can you tell us whether or not that's how you recall it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can state that I may have been wrong as much as a few months and I am prepared to accept your proposition. It concerns the organs of the MUP, and there must be some documentation to corroborate when the republican president was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Colonel Pesic, I have very few questions for you, and I think we can probably get through them fairly rapidly. The first issue that I would like to address is the subordination, the resubordination of the military district to the Pristina Corps, and in that connection I'd like you to look at a document which you predicted during your testimony must exist, and that is 4D85. I think you can see that document on your screen now. Now, this is a document dated the 8th of April of 1999, and I think this is the document that you were predicting must exist that deals with the subordination to the Pristina Corps. Am I correct in that regard?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. That's it. This is a well-known document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. And the document provides, does it not, that -- that this resubordination was effective at 0600 hours on April 7th of 1999; correct? You'll see that in the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness was inaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You have to answer the question again; they weren't able to hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you give your --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree that this document concerns resubordination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, does it not actually refer to an earlier order which is the effective one -- well, this is giving effect to it but there must be a 3rd Army order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is, it refers to that order, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the dates shown --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The 3rd Army order was April 7th. This one is the 8th. It's just passing it -- in the normal chain of command, they come all the way down through the chain and finally get to this level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And what I wanted to establish was the date, Your Honour, and I think we've done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'd like you now to look at another document -- this document is -- well, just while we're on this document, look up in the upper left-hand corner and you'll see where it says under Pristina Corps command there are some numbers, 455-130. Now, it's the case, isn't it, that those numbers 455-130, the 455 tells you that that is an order coming from the Pristina Corps, and then 130 is just the number of that particular order. That's the way those numbers work, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further down in the text I read: "Based on orders of the command of the 3rd Army number 3372-1 of 7 April," therefore what Mr. Bonomy asked me, based on this -- that order, the Pristina Corps command drafted this order on the resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I think you've misunderstood my question or it may have not been translated properly to you. My question really is that number 455 up there at the top, if you knew nothing else, that number would tell you that it is an order coming from the Pristina Corps, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were given a preceding document with that number, I could answer. There is a log-book with the Pristina Corps command where you have all the numbers in sequence. I don't know about the numbers. All I can say is that this is an order on the resubordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure we're communicating. For instance, when you issued orders from the military district, those orders were always preceded with the identifier for the military district, which was number 139. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't have to be like that. I don't have much experience with registers and log-books. I'm not sure. I cannot answer this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. So you don't -- somebody else would put those numbers in there and you weren't responsible for them I guess is the position you're taking and we can move on from that.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is a bookkeeping matter, that of log-books. It concerns documents only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand. We can deal with that with someone else. The one thing I do want to point out in that regard is with document P1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I'd like to have that brought up, please. P1968.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You saw this document earlier today, and I think you'll recall without having to look at it that it's a document, if you look at the last page, that purports to be a document of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija. Do you see that? And then if we go back and look at the first page, and if we're correct that the number 455 designates Pristina Corps, this document was issued under the 445 [sic] number of the Pristina Corps 455-73; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that this order has been entered in the log-book at all because it hasn't got a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's not -- we have to scroll up to the top and then you'll see the number.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I now want to look at another document, P1415, that you've also seen earlier today. The first thing I want to draw your attention to with regard to this document, and this is a document that's issued by General Pavkovic while he was commander of the Pristina Corps, if you look at the first paragraph, you see that this issue was ordered pursuant to an order of the 3rd Army, order number 168-104 of 26 June 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And based upon your knowledge of the chain of command, I take it you would also agree that that order issued by the 3rd Army had to be either issued originally by the Chief of Staff of the General Staff or approved by the General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is not clear to me. Does it refer to this document alone or to the previous document and this one? This document is issued pursuant to an order of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, and my question -- and I may not be asking them precisely. We saw documents earlier today. One of those documents, you might recall, was a request by General Pavkovic when he was 3rd Army commander to the General Staff to resubordinate certain units of the military district. That request was then approved by the General Staff and then the resubordination order was issued. What I'm asking you about this particular document was that before the 3rd Army could issue this order, they would have had to have approval from the General Staff, the Chief of the General Staff, or they were issuing an order pursuant to an order of the Chief of the General Staff. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me to do the job of an expert witness rather than an ordinary witness. There are issues which are in the purview of the army commander and others which are in the purview of the corps commander. But I cannot be precise in my answer because I don't want to cause confusion. The competences of the army commander are clear and of the staff, but I am unable to assist here with a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Chief of Staff rather than staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You've given your answer and thank you. You've had plenty of opportunity to study this order. Do you see anything in that order that orders something illegal?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the entire order, the contents of the order?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yeah, does the order order someone to do something illegal? Is there anything illegal ordered by that document? There's not, is there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The competences are strictly regulated at each level, but I do not wish to be an expert witness. I cannot comment. I'm sure that everybody issues the order he's authorised to issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this doesn't require you to be an expert witness. You are a -- you were a colonel in the army and you knew, as a colonel in the army, that you were duty-bound to carry out any order you received unless that order was illegal. Now, if that -- this order had been issued to you, would you have felt duty-bound to carry it out, or do you see something in it that would be illegal and justify you to refuse to carry it out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would carry out this order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does not conflict -- it does not conflict with the basic principles of command and what can and cannot be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to look now at document P1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis was showing you this document today and asking you about your knowledge of it, and you talked about a unit here that had something to do with anti-aircraft. Is that true? Is there an anti-aircraft unit involved here?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, no. There was actually no anti-aircraft unit involved here, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. What is the nature of the unit that they're trying to relocate away from a populated area? What kind of a unit is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are military territorial units, mostly infantry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, this -- this issue was ordered on the 23rd of April of 1999; that was during the period of the NATO bombing, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And if one wanted to protect the civilians in those villages from NATO bombing, it might be wise to move military units out of those villages because they were the targets of NATO bombing, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know if you had any responsibility at all as commander of the military district for reservists of the MUP. Were you responsible for MUP reservists?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Responsibility in the sense of bringing up to manpower levels at their request.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But that was simply a matter of supplying bodies at the request of MUP. You didn't have any supervisory authority over people who were previously designated as MUP reservists, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the meeting that Mr. O'Sullivan talked to you about that you were invited to by General Pavkovic, he spoke about your -- your update to your statement, your supplemental information sheet. And you dealt with paragraph 32 in that supplemental information sheet, and you said that you and Pavkovic were only passive participants of that meeting; in other words, you were the audience basically. Neither one of you participated in any way, did you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes you agree with what I said?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. One final question. You talked about the two bodies that were found in the industrial zone, and you were asked if they were wearing civilian clothing. And I want to ask you this question: Based upon your experience, was it possible to identify a KLA member by whether they were wearing a uniform or civilian clothes? Was that a way you could identify a KLA member?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer with any precision because I did not have any occasion to run into members of the KLA. I assume that some had uniforms and some didn't, but this description indicates that they were civilians and this was in the first few days of the bombing. So we concluded that this had been a show-down connected with looting of buildings. These were buildings that had a lot of goods in them, and we concluded that they were the victims of a show-down. Nearby we found that some business premises had been looted. This happened on the 25th or the 26th. I can't be very precise about the date, but it was in the first few days of the bombing when individuals took the opportunity to try looting. And we concluded that this had been a show-down among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Mr. Pesic. My name is Mihajlo Bakrac, an attorney-at-law, one of the Defence counsel for General Lazarevic. I will skip over the first page of my notes because I think we have already cleared up the time when the resubordination of the territorial units to the Pristina Corps took place. What I'm interested in now, sir, is whether according to the rules of combat -- well, in fact, first I'll ask you the following. You said that in wartime the military sectors were subordinated to the brigades and that as a commander of the military district you had no command responsibility over the units. Were all the units subordinated to the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the order we saw here, it says that they're resubordinated to the military -- to the Pristina Corps. This referred to the military district and the base, the entire military district and the 202nd base were subordinated to the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: According to the rules of combat, could lower-level units from some be resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The rules provide for the resubordination of levels, of units, perhaps not to the same level of command, but commands of the same level are resubordinated, or rather, there's no resubordination envisaged but in this situation the brigade commands are responsible for their area in which there were military sectors, which is why the military sectors were resubordinated to the brigades which were part of the corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, you're both using the same language, and therefore we need to be conscious of the need to have a break between the end of the question and the beginning of the answer and also between the end of the answer and the beginning of the question. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best not to overstep the time-limit and yet meet the demands of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, would you agree with me if I were to tell you that on the 1st of May, 1999, out of 24 detachments, which in your statement you say existed within the territorial district, only 11 detachments were resubordinated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resubordination of a military sector implied the resubordination of the detachments within it. You may have come across a document which lists only some particular detachments which were resubordinated initially. However, the resubordination of the Prizren military sector implied the resubordination of all the detachments.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Without enumerating each individual detachment, is there a possibility that some detachments were not used and did not participate in the tasks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to the brigade commander in his area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, is that a suitable point to interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, any advance on this question of whether there will be any response to the application for a videolink? Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have discussed it among ourselves, and what concerns us is, first, that as a rule I feel that a witness of such importance should not be questioned through videolink. The witness is mentioned in the indictment many times and he's very important, especially for the fate of Sainovic. However, bearing in mind that we wish to expedite the proceedings, I never oppose anything proposed by the OTP which could facilitate this. The issue is the health of this person. I will not go into it because it's confidential, but I believe that his witness -- that his health will be at risk. And in our area he could not be a witness and testify. So I require three days to think about it. He has to have a medical check-up on the 9th of December. If on the 9th of December he is told it's all right, we will take the risk; otherwise, I am afraid that there may be dire consequences. Therefore, I would not like to express my -- any position right now as to whether we support this or not, because it says here that the medical check-up is to take place in a month, which means the 9th of December. And then maybe in the last week of December this can be done, if it has to be done. But I would not like to take any position until Monday. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'll deal with that in just a second. We have to break shortly, Mr. Pesic, so could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood you, Mr. Fila, but you left me with the impression that you might be suggesting that for medical reasons the witness should not testify at all. Is that what you envisage?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm afraid that if I were to agree I would have this man on my conscience. I do want him to testify but want him to be fit to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that. Are there any circumstances, though, in which you envisage insisting that he comes to The Hague to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think he is an important witness, as Your Honour has said, and that for this reason he should be here. But if he's really ill - and I have no reason to disbelieve it - then I don't think that he should not testify; and therefore, I would agree with Mr. Hannis's proposal that this be done by videolink. If the OTP thinks it's a good idea, then it's a good idea. But I do not want to take the risk of agreeing to his testifying in his present condition. And you will see for yourself that he is to have a medical check-up on the 9th of December, and then we will see whether he is fit to testify; and if he's fit to travel, he can come here; if not, we can do it by videolink. But we only received this yesterday. I am not saying that he should not testify. On the contrary, I agree with Your Honour that he is a very important witness, but I cannot agree with this situation right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a little bit different concern. This is an important witness and a witness that I think we're all working about one or two witnesses ahead is about as far as we can go because of the pace. When you suggested that this witness may be part of a videolink as early as next week and the problem with that is when you're doing a videolink you must supply any documents you want to use with that witness substantially in advance of their testimony. I have an e-mail from Mr. Haider saying that he would like any documents by Monday. I think it would be difficult for me to go through all the material I have to go through with regard to Witness Loncar and come up with the documents I might want to put to him and have them in Mr. Haider's hands by Monday. I think that might be quite difficult. So that's just a practical concern. I have no objection to him testifying by videolink. I think that the motion makes out a case for that. While I'm on my feet, may I raise another matter or would you prefer that I do it later?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, go on now with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this refers to the witness that is currently on the stand, and it is a matter that I think is of some concern. The night before he took the witness-stand we got about an eight-page new statement that had been given to UNMIK by this witness. It turns out that that statement is of little moment in terms of this witness's testimony, but we were informed that it was a statement that had recently come to the attention of the Prosecution. I inquired into that and learned that it had been given to the Prosecution in June before the trial even started and was part of eight volumes of documents that were supplied to the Prosecution by UNMIK. The explanation was that the record search with regard to the witnesses had been done in May, and since the documents didn't arrive here until June it wasn't until they were contemplating calling this particular witness that they did another search and discovered this document. And that is alarming to me for this reason. It would seem to me if the Prosecution got eight volumes of documents from UNMIK that would raise an immediate red flag that they ought to be carefully considered because this is a Kosovo case and that they obviously have to do with Kosovo. The deeper concern I have about that is whether or not within that eight volumes of documents there's Rule 68 material that should have been turned over to us some time ago, whether there's other material that could contribute to the furtherance of justice in this case. It may be symptomatic of what Mr. Hannis and I and the other counsel for the accused here have been saying to you over and over in motions, is that we're not getting adequate preparation time, and therefore things we should be doing are not getting done, things are falling through the cracks, and I think this -- I am convinced the Prosecution wasn't playing any games with us, that what they tell us happened happened exactly that way. We are all very overwhelmed with the work we have to do, and we're just not getting done the things we should be doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I interrupt you there because there are no tangible signs of the problem that you repeatedly raise and we have indicated to you that there will be time in due course, if necessary, when we will explore or allow interruptions to enable points that can be established to be investigated. This particular issue is one which when you've had an opportunity to explore it fully with the Prosecution you should raise with us if there remains a particular matter that requires our attention. And I think that ought to be done in a written filing. Meanwhile, we'll adjourn and we'll resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Bring the witness in, please. On the videolink application the Defence should respond, if they intend to, by Monday in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, we stopped at the issue of the detachments which had been resubordinated to the brigades according to the rules of engagement and for a longer period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard the witness say "yes." Perhaps that should be recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the witness say anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just carry on, please, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, I'm interested in something else now, and it will be important once the Defence case begins. I wanted to clarify something that is found in paragraph 7 of your statement. You said that in 1999 the Pristina Corps was commanded by Mr. Lazarevic and that assistant commander for morale was Colonel Starcevic. Would it refresh your memory if I said that in 1999 assistant commander for morale in the corps was Colonel Marinkovic rather than Stankovic. Stankovic was assistant commander with the 3rd Army. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would. This is a matter of a few months and there were shifts, people moved about, and I may have mixed things up after seven years. These are facts we are talking about. There are orders in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, I'm not criticising you in any way, but if we have these witnesses here tomorrow we have to have a clear picture as to their positions. You also stated that the assistant for operations was Colonel Djakovic. Would you agree with me if I said that the chief of operations was Colonel Stefanovic and that Djakovic was in the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with that as well. These were the moves made immediately prior. I don't know whether it was at the end of 1998 or early 1999, but there were changes within the corps and I accept anything that can be verified by facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, to repeat, I'm not criticising you; I just wanted to have this clear on the record and it suffices that you confirm you agree so that we can move more quickly. Is it also correct, as you stated in paragraph 7, that Colonel Stefanovic was the Chief of Staff of the corps? Would you agree if I said that the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps in 1999 was Colonel Zivkovic and not Colonel Stefanovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some shifts in a short period there as well. There was a colonel whose name I cannot recall. He was there for a brief period, and then the changes continued. It is possible I was mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. To move to another topic, or rather, I will follow your statement. In paragraphs 10 and 11, you discuss the bringing up to strength of the Pristina Corps by using reservists. Would you agree with me that when we talk about 1999 and the time of war, the Pristina Corps was, to a large extent, brought up to strength ex-territorially with people from outside of Kosovo due to the lack of sufficient numbers of military-aged men of some certain specialties in Kosovo itself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree and I believe I mentioned that, that the predominantly ex-territorial principle was used to bring the Pristina Corps up to strength.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we clarify one thing regarding the bringing up to strength. You mentioned the law on mobilisation as stipulating that the military sector was tasked with sending conscripts to the Army of Yugoslavia, to the MUP, and to the civilian protection, if I understood correctly.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Pesic, that the reason for the use of reservists to bring the MUP up to strength was that there was a general shortage and that you deployed MUP reservists upon their request and based on their choice?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge as regards that is limited. I spent a short time in that position because shortly afterwards there was the 24th of March. Subsequently, dealing with certain issues, I did notice some examples of good cooperation with the MUP and not so good cooperation; namely, certain MUP stations and certain MUP bodies took the liberty of taking the men themselves by or through private channels, by knowing them. And such people had their wartime deployment, which was different. And they -- and I tried to resolve these issues immediately prior to the 24th or maybe once the aggression, the bombings, had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I agree, but let me interrupt you. Therefore, they were part of the record, but as for the supply of materiel, uniform, weaponry, they received those from the MUP?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And at the moment when they became the reservists of the MUP, they were under no command of the VJ. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. This is what I wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, page 67, line 11 -- no, 13 and 14. My question was that the MUP reservists were also part of the record with the military sectors for the reasons of simplicity, to have a unified record, whereas the interpretation was that there was a due to a general lack of men [as interpreted]. That was not my intention. I wanted to show that there was an attempt to unify, or rather, have a single register of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't have the place for this, Mr. Bakrac, where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 67, lines 13 and 14.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's to do with bringing the MUP up to strength, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. My question was whether the MUP reservists were also part of the record with the military sectors so that there would be a unified register of conscripts and not because of the shortage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's so far removed from what's on the transcript that you should ask the question again to clarify the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I was hoping that the subsequent questions cleared it up, but let us deal with that detail --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: As long as you're happy that they have, but there's no way I can sort out that mistake, and if you think it still needs to be sorted out you'll need to ask the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, to repeat -- to ask you once again: Is it correct that the MUP reservists were also on the records of the military sectors so that there would be a unified record of conscripts or of able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on. Mr. Pesic, would you also agree with me, if you have any such knowledge, that throughout the time of war all units of the Pristina Corps did not mobilise the entire reserve force because they were able to increase the number of recruits serving their military term and that the mobilisation of certain portions of the units was also done in May 1999?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since it was the task of the military sectors, I do not have an extensive knowledge about it. But I know that there were such instances. The problem was the shortage of vehicles and not so much the shortage of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you know, Mr. Pesic, that a significant number of military conscripts from Kosovo and Metohija remained -- did not get mobilised until the end of the war because their specialties did not correspond to the needs of the corps units?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such instances, and I could see it for myself. I could see some of those people hanging out in various cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it also correct that those who had not been mobilised were those conscripts who had had their uniforms and equipment from an earlier period?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once placed, they remained in such units where commanders took more care to plan and then they would ask for replenishment from the ranks of some younger men. Therefore, some older people remained in units for a longer time, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: We may not have understood each other. Is it correct that there was a number of conscripts who were not mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is, therefore, that whether these conscripts were those who had been issued with uniforms before, as reservists, before the war. They had it at home?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly there were some, but they were earlier generations. They were not re-called to return uniforms, although they were taken off the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: That was what I meant. Did you have occasion to see such not-mobilised members wearing uniforms while you were moving around?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not unusual to see people, men, wearing parts of uniform, not complete uniforms, but wearing either the top or the trousers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When -- when and where would you see people wearing parts of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One could see them every day. They used it as normal clothes, which I believe was the subject of an order that was issued I don't know exactly when but it was issued by, I believe, the corps commander who stipulated in that order that the matter should be taken under watch and that such people should be prevented from going around wearing parts of uniforms. I think such an order existed. I can't remember in which period. But this phenomenon had been observed and I believe it was the subject of an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you saw this happening every day, what action did you take about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, you would see them in passing, driving by. You would see people in the street. Those were individual cases, and I didn't think it made sense to stop and tackle such people on the spot, to ask them where they got the uniform, why they were wearing it. I personally did not take any measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One hears of responsible military officers when they encounter indiscipline seeking name, rank, and number and then following it up later. Nothing of that nature was done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm trying to say is that there is an order, an instruction or recommendation, to take steps, and those steps could have been taken only by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think the interpreter missed one detail. The witness said that those persons were mainly unarmed. We can check it on the tape. But it would be on the page 71, between lines 14 and 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It didn't cross my mind that being armed was an issue here, and therefore I'm happy to accept what you say. What disturbs me, Mr. Pesic, is the attitude I think I've heard before in this case that if there's an order requiring something to be done, then everyone else can wash their hands of it. Was that the general approach, that this was a military police matter and therefore another officer like you could just wash your hand of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What matters is a specific judgement in a specific case. You can encounter a poor peasant who's using this as cheap clothing. He's using it as long as it's in his possession, as long as it's available. It's a judgement call. You have to make a quick assessment of what kind of individual that is, whether he has a purpose in wearing that uniform or he's just wearing it for no reason, no particular reason at all, or if it's a case of abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, is it also correct that certain military conscripts from military territorial detachments were relieved from units at the beginning of the war to help out in utility companies, in security details on important facilities, as civilians during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did feel certain pressure of that kind because there were some military conscripts who were indispensable to normal life in town. They were indispensable to the population, both the Serbs and the Albanians. Businesses could not operate without them, bakeries could not operate without this personnel. At one point, there was even a shortage of personnel in cemeteries. There was no one available to dig graves, so we had to relieve personnel from their normal military duties to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You spoke of your personal efforts in engaging Albanians in mobilisation drives. You spoke of that. You will agree then if I say that there was never any coercive mobilisation of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a good intention to set up a unit of that kind and send a message to renegade groups that they do not enjoy the sympathies of even their own citizens, their own fellow countrymen. Some were willing to join, but most were not. Some were willing to accept weapons as long as nobody found out about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So they feared extremists among their own ethnic community?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's why they felt reluctant to become part of such a detachment, which we intended to call the Albanian Territorial Detachment. And the unemployment of Albanians in socially owned enterprises was 100 per cent in all age groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that there were any volunteer detachments among the Goranis, for instance?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had information from the military department of Prizren that they did get organised and that they were joined, integrated, into one of our territorial detachments called Gora that grew at one point from 370 men to close to 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. You spoke about the commandeering of machines and equipment from individuals and enterprises, businesses. Do you know that under the Law of Mobilisation and according to a decree issued by the Federal Government, it was a legal possibility envisaged by the law?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course that was a legal, planned activity of the military department which was supposed to move to the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Defence precisely in that period. However, we dealt with it because we had the necessary records of commandeered vehicles from either private persons or companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that activity was planned back in peacetime; it was not an ad hoc activity undertaken suddenly in the state of war.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same kind of planned activity as the mobilisation of conscripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And did the military department of Pristina and the Pristina Corps, in enforcing this obligation, act totally within the law?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We, but we did not comply with all the requirements and obligations of the Pristina Corps because of a shortage of vehicles. They did exist on paper, in planning documents. We had files for those vehicles, but the condition of the vehicles was not good enough to meet the requirements of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. At the beginning of this last answer we should have a "yes." If I understood you correctly, Mr. Pesic, the planned -- it was planned to commandeer many more vehicles than were actually commandeered during the war?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This activity was conducted in keeping with the strictly prescribed actual requirements of the units, and we did the planning aspect of the job in peacetime. But at the moment when mobilisation started, we did not fully implement the plan because when inspecting the vehicles we realised their condition was either not satisfactory or their profile did not correspond to the requirements of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'll ask you one more thing that needs to be clarified on the record. We spoke about a unit at Dragas, and it's on the record that a volunteer detachment was formed. What I understood is that those people were mobilised on a voluntary basis.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a territorial detachment in Dragas that was built up with volunteers from that area, and that's why it grew to the number I mentioned, almost 600.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you've finished with that question, can I ask you, when you commandeered a vehicle, how did you mark it to show that it was a military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There exists regulations governing the marking of such vehicles. Planning documents were prepared in peacetime for such vehicles, and when commandeered they are placed on record, accepted by a commission, and they are marked with a triangle, with a certain lettering, Army of Yugoslavia. And that was a sign that the vehicle had been requisitioned, commandeered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is that triangle displayed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the wind-screen, visibly. On the right-hand side of the driver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that when the vehicle was driven along the road at a reasonable speed, an outside observer would never know whether it was a military commandeered vehicle or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those triangles were visible. Their size was quite adequate. It was easy to notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Something that's easy to notice on a wind-screen is going to interfere with the visibility of the driver, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not in front of the driver; they were in front of the passenger seat on the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, is it correct that up to 1998 the entity that had the military obligation -- that handled the military obligation was the military district in a certain area and then in 1998/1999 that was taken over by the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the commandeering of vehicles, it was a transition period, and that's exactly when the bombing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I asked about the materiel obligation and not military obligation in my last question. That was page 76, line 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you were referring to the commandeering of vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was talking about the materiel obligation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Which would in English, interpreter's note, mean something like property liability.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: The obligation to provide property for the requirements of the army. That was or that became one of the competences of the Ministry of Defence in 1998/1999.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The preparation was done by the Ministry of Defence in peacetime for wartime needs, securing materiel reserves for the needs of military units. Specifically speaking of vehicles, they were in the jurisdiction of military districts and military departments. In 1998, this particular duty was supposed to be taken over by the bodies of the Ministry of Defence. However, the transition was never implemented and the vehicles remained within the jurisdiction of military districts and departments. However, the preparation was done by the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, you testified that some of these units were used to some extent. Do you know, do you have information, about the losses during the war in your military district? I'm speaking only about the members of these units.

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Out of the members of the military district, 54 were killed and 108 were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And that's about 0.4 per cent of the total?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 0.3 or 0.4 per cent, because the total strength varied precisely because our -- because of our duty to relieve some conscripts for other jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the members were mainly engaged in security duties, securing facilities, installations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part. Most of them were killed or wounded during ambushes and explosions on roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You also testified that the military district received daily combat reports. You received daily combat reports. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not regularly because of the prevailing situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Meaning that the communications were often in trouble during the war and sometimes did not function during the war for several days running?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and sometimes only courier communications were available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your question about the losses during the war -- oh, yes, sorry, I missed the words "during the war." It's clear in fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is it also correct, Mr. Pesic, that not a single military territorial unit had any village defence duties?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically because the detachment was made up of men from several villages in one municipality, and they were protecting the property of one specific municipality. The prevailing principle in establishment was the municipal principle. A small municipality like Klina could only set up a small detachment of two companies. That was the whole municipality of Klina, consisting of several villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And their duties involved mostly securing important facilities and installations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were asked previously, and also shown a document of the 549th Motorised Brigade, referring to an order of the Pristina Corps. Do you remember an order of the Pristina Corps commander to the effect that military territorial units should abandon population centres and the cited reason was that they should avoid air-strikes targeting military positions, to organise defence from ground aggression, and to enable the civilian population to continue normal life during the war, diminishing the risks?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that order. Decisions were made depending on the specific situation of each detachment and each territory. Specifically I can say that the Podujevo detachment was never in Podujevo; it was always busy securing other installations and facilities outside, because there are no strategic facilities in Podujevo as a municipality, they were mostly in Pristina securing water-supply facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You were asked -- and I'm going to show you a Defence exhibit related to that. You were asked by Mr. Hannis in examination-in-chief about the civilian protection staff and whether you were a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see in e-court, please, Defence Exhibit 5D29. I believe we have it in English and in Serbian, and I would appreciate it if we could see them both.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you see on the left-hand side, Mr. Pesic, it reads: "Decision. Pursuant to the decision to form a temporary Executive Council," and then it specifies the members. "The decision is made to form the staff to coordinate activities of the civilian structures for the area of the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija." Is this the staff you testified about, the staff of civilian protection which is actually called the staff for the coordination of the work of the civilian structures?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that I've never seen this decision. In my personal contact with Mr. Petar Ilic and with Mr. Dragan Markovic, I learned that I was a member of that provincial staff. And then I relayed this to General Lazarevic as soon as I could, and I sought his permission to attend the meetings of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In item 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could scroll down.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: -- as regards the task of the staff, it reads: "Based on demonstrated need and conditions of war and aimed at better organised assessment and resolution of significant issues and the functioning and coordination of all structures in the province, the staff is entrusted with monitoring on a daily basis and taking adequate measures in the supply of energy, consumer goods, vital foodstuffs, medicines, medical supplies, health care services, taking possession of goods," and so on and so forth. Did these measures encompass the entire population of Kosovo and Metohija, including the Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we supplied shops in various towns in Pristina itself and other settlements, then anyone could go there and get goods. There was never a particular type of distribution to the Serbian population in this or that location. However, we did target certain Albanian groups who were out of their settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: It is also mentioned that the goods will be distributed for humanitarian needs. Would this imply what you've just stated?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Part of the goods was distributed through trade companies, so as to avoid abuse. It would officially be forwarded to a trading company, which would then put the goods in their records and distribute it to the overall population. As for the fleeing Albanian population, such goods were distributed in places where they were at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pesic. You mentioned Mr. Petar Ilic and you said he was the provincial secretary on behalf of the Ministry of Defence. Is it correct that at that time he was also the chief of the secretariat of defence of Pristina, tasked with the protection of civilians and -- of population and property and that he was subordinated to the Ministry of Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it's -- this sums it up. I don't know his exact function. But as regards peacetime as assistant commander for logistics, I dealt with such issues in my contact with him as regards supply of units. I cooperated with some of his organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pesic, in paragraph 22 of your statement -- or, rather, in paragraph 24 you state that certain parts of the 3rd Army staff were deployed to Pristina. Did you have in mind the forward command post of the 3rd Army or some other parts of that command?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our rules of engagement, such situations are envisaged, and yes, I could call it a forward command post, and its existence would be fully justified under the circumstances. I welcomed that move because I could deal with many issues concerning supply in a quicker manner because I had the people I needed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And who was there at the forward command post on behalf of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe the commander himself was there at a certain point, the commander of the 3rd Army, General Samardzic. Then there was General Stanmirovic [phoen] at a certain point, but I wasn't much interested in that. I was interested in the logistics bodies which were there because I had to deal with them within my competences. And there were people from various branches or various services of the logistics there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. We are talking about the time of war in 1999. Is it also correct that the command of the Pristina Corps could be found in several locations and that these locations changed constantly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were moments when I didn't know where the command of the Pristina Corps was. However, their courier always knew where to find me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm not a military expert, but I will venture a question. Was use of camouflage justified in such situation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For that level of decision-making, I believe the decisions made were proper. However, I stubbornly refused to move from where I was because I knew it was an important facility for the entire province and that there would be no bombing, no strikes against that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I presume you have in mind the library?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the building. It's a separate building having a commanding view of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: However, your personnel in the library was unarmed. You used the unarmed members of your command?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My command comprises -- comprised 56 men, out of which there were ten women, around 20 civilians who began wearing uniforms as of the moment of their mobilisation and they lived nearby. So as to prevent possible losses, I allowed most of them to spend their nights at home, for the reason of safety of their families; and only the minimum number of people remained at the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, but they were unarmed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had side-arms, hand-guns, and I always had a few policemen close by but they were not highly visible. They were within the building itself, though, and you couldn't see a single police vehicle anywhere near the building, and I also had a civilian policeman on board -- policeman in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Bakrac please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked to repeat that question, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesic, in peacetime and outside of Kosovo and Metohija, was it also normal that military sectors were housed in civilian buildings instead of military buildings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended on the conditions, but they were never in barracks. Sometimes they would be with the command of the garrison or in some civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: For the most part, they were with the Municipal Assemblies?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the previous stage when the military sectors were under Municipal Assemblies, yes. And for the most part, civilians were employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 26 you mentioned 1998. Is it correct -- well, first of all, there is something that isn't clear and I wanted to clarify that with you. You say that the Pristina Corps in 1998 had one forward command post in Djakovica and the Pristina Corps commander, Lazarevic, was usually there. This could be read in two ways. I wanted to clarify this. Isn't it correct that in 1998 the then-Colonel Lazarevic was Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and that in Djakovica there was a forward command post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are correct. I believe that this is a matter of translation or a typing error. I believe it is sufficiently clear. I agree with you that he, as the Chief of Staff, was in Djakovica for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you were asked about that by my learned friend Mr. Hannis, and he was referred to as the deputy commander; however, he was the Chief of Staff of the Pristina Corps and he was at the forward command post in 1998 in Djakovica. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Did you also know that the then-Colonel, and now General, Lazarevic in 1998 as of April until the end of that year was in Djakovica at the forward command post and that there was no possibility to leave that forward command post?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You've testified on 1998 already, and you dealt with during your examination-in-chief and your touring of the forward command post. In paragraph 28 you say that there was a command post in Djakovica in 1999, and you probably have the same forward command post in mind. And you say that on one occasion you went to see Colonel Zivkovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we agree that Colonel Zivkovic was at the forward command post in Djakovica throughout 1999 and he was the -- one of the chiefs of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZLATOMIR PESIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is so. I believe he was there throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: You've also stated that when touring Djakovica and Prizren in April and May 1999 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a correction for the transcript. Line 24, page 85 -- no, sorry, line 3, it should read: "As the Chief of Staff" -- [In English] One of the chiefs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wonder if this is a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I was hoping you were nearing the end, Mr. Bakrac. Have we long to go with you?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you've held it against me once already and I had no time to apologise and explain. In our jurisdiction we make no time assessments, and I'm particularly bad at it. And I don't want to speculate. If I provide you with an assessment, I may well go wrong because I'm not very well versed in it, but I believe half an hour, 45 minutes for me to conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's certainly going to be way over what we had envisaged, Mr. Bakrac. So I ask you and the others who have to follow you to look closely at what is necessary in view of what substance has emerged from the evidence of this witness. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't want to -- I'm sorry. I didn't want to interrupt while my colleague was cross-examining the witness. On page 73, line 14, I believe it's important, the witness said when he was talking the -- why the Albanians were reluctant to join the army he said they feared the retribution or the revenge from the extremists. And maybe the witness can be asked about that. He clearly said that, but it didn't show in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which line are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 73, 14. Page 73, line 14. When he was giving the reasons why the Albanians were reluctant to join the army. He said they feared retribution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I note what you say, but I think the answer is there. Because the question is: So they feared extremists among their own ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But I note what you say. I doubt if it really significantly alters the context of his answer. Thank you. We've been unable to finish your evidence today, Mr. Pesic, so you're required to return tomorrow to continue; that will be at 2.15. Please remember what I said to you last night that you don't have any discussion with anybody about any aspect of your evidence until you return here tomorrow at 2.15. Now could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 2.15 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of November, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
